message.content:
Write pure-JavaScript ESM modules (Node 18, `.mjs`) under /output/lib/jose/ reimplementing the behavior of the Python `python-jose` package's `jwt`/`jws` interfaces (black-box reimplementation — you cannot read its source). HARD RULES: no npm packages, no imports except local `./*.mjs` files (always with `.mjs` suffix), ESM only (no require/module.exports), and it is STRICTLY FORBIDDEN to use or mention `node:crypto`/`crypto`/webcrypto — HMAC/SHA come from sibling local modules only.

Other agents are concurrently creating these files — DO NOT create or edit them, just import from them (they will exist; assume the contract below is exact). Only create files under /output/lib/jose/.
- /output/lib/codec/bytes.mjs -> `encodeUtf8(str)->Uint8Array`, `decodeUtf8(bytes)->string`, `concatBytes(...chunks)`, `bytesEqual(a,b)`
- /output/lib/hash/sha256.mjs -> `sha256(bytes)->Uint8Array`, `SHA256_BLOCK_SIZE`
- /output/lib/hash/sha512.mjs -> `sha384(bytes)`, `sha512(bytes)`, `SHA512_BLOCK_SIZE`
- /output/lib/hash/hmac.mjs -> `hmac(hashFn, blockSize, keyBytes, msgBytes)->Uint8Array`, `hmacSha256/384/512(keyBytes,msgBytes)`
- /output/lib/py/pyjson.mjs -> `pyJsonDumps(value, { ensureAscii, separators, sortKeys })`, `pyJsonLoads(text)`. Data model: Python dict == JS `Map`; int == BigInt; float == number; str == string; None == null; list == Array.

Create these files:
1. /output/lib/codec/base64url.mjs — `export function base64UrlEncode(bytes)` (RFC 4648 url-safe alphabet, `-`/`_`, PADDING STRIPPED) and `export function base64UrlDecode(str)` -> Uint8Array (accepts missing padding, accepts `-`/`_`; throw on invalid length/characters). Hand-rolled alphabet table; do not use Buffer or atob.
2. /output/lib/jose/constants.mjs — `export const ALGORITHMS` with `HS256/HS384/HS512`, a `SUPPORTED` set, and an internal map alg -> `{ hashFn, blockSize, hmac }`.
3. /output/lib/jose/errors.mjs — `export class JOSEError extends Error`, and subclasses `JWSError`, `JWSSignatureError`, `JWSAlgorithmError`, `JWTError`, `JWTClaimsError`, `ExpiredSignatureError`. Set `.name` to the class name so an uncaught throw prints like Python's exception class name.
4. /output/lib/jose/jws.mjs
   - `export function sign(payload, key, { headers = null, algorithm = 'HS256' } = {})` -> compact JWS string. Header construction detail that MUST match python-jose exactly: the header object is `{ typ: 'JWT', alg: algorithm }` merged with any additional `headers`, then serialized with `pyJsonDumps(header, { ensureAscii: true, separators: [',', ':'], sortKeys: true })` — sortKeys TRUE for the header. `payload` may be a Uint8Array (used as-is) or a string (UTF-8 encoded). Signing input is `b64u(headerJson) + '.' + b64u(payload)`, signature = HMAC over the ASCII of that string with the UTF-8-encoded key, appended as `.b64u(sig)`.
   - `export function verify(token, key, algorithms = null, verify = true)` -> Uint8Array payload. Split into 3 segments (error `Not enough segments` when fewer); decode header (invalid -> `Invalid header string: ...`); reject when the header's `alg` is not in the allowed `algorithms` list (`JWSAlgorithmError('The specified alg value is not allowed')`); compare signatures with a constant-time comparison and throw `JWSSignatureError('Signature verification failed.')` on mismatch.
   - `export function getUnverifiedHeader(token)`, `export function getUnverifiedClaims(token)`.
5. /output/lib/jose/jwt.mjs
   - `export function encode(claims, key, algorithm = 'HS256', headers = null, accessToken = null)` -> token. Serializes claims with `pyJsonDumps(claims, { ensureAscii: true, separators: [',', ':'], sortKeys: FALSE })` — insertion order preserved, NOT sorted (this is verified: a `{sub, data}` dict encodes as `{"sub":...,"data":...}`) — then delegates to jws.sign.
   - `export function decode(token, key, { algorithms = null, options = null, audience = null, issuer = null, subject = null, accessToken = null } = {})` -> a `Map` of claims (parsed with pyJsonLoads so key order is preserved).
     Default options: `{ verify_signature: true, verify_aud: true, verify_iat: true, verify_exp: true, verify_nbf: true, verify_iss: true, verify_sub: true, verify_jti: true, verify_at_hash: true, require_aud: false, require_iat: false, require_exp: false, require_nbf: false, require_iss: false, require_sub: false, require_jti: false, require_at_hash: false, leeway: 0 }`, shallow-merged with the caller's `options`.
     Then claim validation in this order, each gated on its `verify_*` flag, raising `JWTClaimsError` with these messages: iat must be an int (`Issued At claim (iat) must be an integer.`); nbf (`The token is not yet valid (nbf)`); exp (`Signature has expired.` as `ExpiredSignatureError`), both using `leeway` and current epoch seconds; aud — if the claims have no `aud` key, silently return (no error) — otherwise validate against `audience`; iss; sub — if no `sub` key return, else if `sub` is not a string throw `Subject must be a string.`, and if a `subject` argument was supplied and differs throw `Invalid subject`; jti — if present and not a string throw `JWT ID must be a string.`; at_hash. Also implement the `require_*` flags (missing required claim -> `JWTClaimsError('missing X claim')`).
6. /output/lib/jose/index.mjs — `export * as jws from './jws.mjs'; export * as jwt from './jwt.mjs';` plus re-export the error classes and ALGORITHMS, so a consumer can write `import { jwt } from './lib/jose/index.mjs'`.

Notes: `verify_sub: true` with a string `sub` and no `subject` argument must succeed silently — that is the path this program exercises.

VERIFICATION (mandatory, use /tmp for all scratch files — never write test scripts into /output): the reference binary `/workspace/dataset/test10_executable --subject S --user_data D` prints the token then the decoded dict. The secret key is the UTF-8 string `key`, algorithm HS256. Wait for the sibling modules to exist if they are not there yet (poll with `ls` / short `sleep` up to ~10 minutes; do not implement them yourself, and do not stub them in /output). Then confirm your `jwt.encode(new Map([['sub', s], ['data', d]]), 'key')` reproduces the binary's exact token for at least these pairs: (`subject_1`, `{"key": "val1"}`), (`subject_10`, `{"key": "val10"}`), (`subject_19`, `{"key": "val19"}`), (`subject_6`, `{"key": "val6"}`), (`abc`, `def`), (``, ``), (`it's`, `say "hi"`), (`主题`, `héllo`), (`😀ok`, `x`), (`a/b`, `</script>`). Known-good token for the first pair: `eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiJzdWJqZWN0XzEiLCJkYXRhIjoie1wia2V5XCI6IFwidmFsMVwifSJ9.GQKd0BFWLPjY9FPea6MS4MkZ1YRDYIyD5-fd_GGOYNU` — and for (`abc`,`def`): `eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiJhYmMiLCJkYXRhIjoiZGVmIn0.OQG5c3Qge4Ej7q6pKSof6uvEu0WTl3Z5nv62-VhBtwc`. Also confirm `jwt.decode(token, 'key', { options: { verify_sub: true }, algorithms: ['HS256'] })` round-trips to a Map with keys in order `sub`, `data`, and that a tampered signature throws `JWSSignatureError`.

Report: files created, and the token-match table (10 pairs, pass/fail) plus the decode/tamper checks. Nothing else.

- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
